nameStory: The Eastern Red Centipede gets its name from its distinctive reddish coloration and its range across eastern North America, including our New England region. The 'red' in its name immediately sets it apart from many other centipedes that tend to be brown or yellowish, making it one of the more colorful members of the centipede family.
description: The Eastern Red Centipede is a large, fast-moving predator that's one of New England's most impressive arthropods. These striking creatures can reach up to 3 inches in length, making them quite substantial compared to most centipedes you'll encounter. They have the classic centipede body plan with many leg-bearing segments, but their reddish coloration makes them stand out. As venomous hunters, they use their speed and bite to capture prey, and they can deliver a painful bite to humans if handled.

idTips.label: Reddish coloration
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive red to reddish-brown body color that gives this centipede its name - it's much more colorful than the typical brown centipedes

idTips.label: Large size
idTips.description: At up to 3 inches long, this is one of the bigger centipedes you'll find in New England - noticeably larger than house centipedes

idTips.label: Swift movement
idTips.description: Moves incredibly quickly when disturbed, with a distinctive rapid, undulating motion that's almost snake-like

idTips.label: Robust body
idTips.description: Feels firm and substantial if you're brave enough to handle one (not recommended!) - not delicate like house centipedes

idTips.label: Many legs
idTips.description: Has 21 pairs of legs (though you probably won't count them in the field!) that move in a wave-like pattern

habitat: Eastern Red Centipedes prefer moist environments and are commonly found under logs, rocks, and leaf litter in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England. They thrive in areas with rich, damp soil where they can hunt for insects, worms, and other small prey. You might also find them in gardens, compost piles, or basement areas where moisture levels are high.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more active as temperatures warm, often found under logs and stones as they hunt for emerging insects and other prey.
seasonality.summer: Most active period when they're easiest to spot during garden work or when moving debris. This is when you're most likely to encounter them.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to seek deeper shelter under logs and rocks as they prepare for winter's chill.
seasonality.winter: Much less active and harder to find, though they don't truly hibernate and may still be discovered in protected spots on warmer days.

funFact: Despite being called a centipede (meaning 'hundred feet'), the Eastern Red Centipede actually has exactly 42 legs - and amazingly, no centipede species actually has 100 legs, with most having anywhere from 30 to 354 legs, but never an even 100!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with millipedes due to its size, but remember that centipedes are fast and aggressive hunters while millipedes are slow decomposers - if it moves quickly and has one pair of legs per body segment, it's your centipede!
contextualKnowledge: Many people fear centipedes more than necessary, but while the Eastern Red Centipede can bite and it is painful, it's not dangerous to humans and these creatures are actually beneficial predators that help control pest insects in gardens and forests.
compareHints: The Eastern Red Centipede is the only member of its genus in New England, making identification easier. Compared to other large centipedes in the region, its reddish coloration is the key distinguishing feature - most other large centipedes tend to be brown, yellow, or darker colored. It's much more robust and colorful than the common house centipede, which is smaller, paler, and has much longer legs.
